Modernism or Postmodernism?

Binswanger, Sullivan, and the Problem of Agency in Contemporary Psychoanalysis*

Roger Frie Psy.D.

Roger Frie

20 West 74th Street
New York, NY 10023
Email: rafrie@yahoo.com

Roger Frie   Department of Psychiatry, St. Luke's-Roosevelt Hospital Center; clinical fellow, William Alanson White Institute.

Clinicians seeking to come to terms with current discussion and debate in psychoanalysis are often confronted with a division between modernism and postmodernism. This bifurcation is essentially a product of the tension between classical and contemporary psychoanalytic traditions and represents the efforts of interpersonal, relational, and intersubjective psychoanalysts to differentiate themselves and their work from their Freudian colleagues. It is also the result of attempts to integrate into psychoanalysis the postmodern intellectual critique of such modernist ideas as subjectivity and individuality.

The distinction between modernism and postmodernism in psychoanalysis takes many forms, affecting the way in which clinicians formulate theory and view technique. The reliance on the analytic neutrality and objectivity that defined classical psychoanalysis has given way to an analytic relationship based on mutuality, in which traditional assumptions about authority and reason yield to ambiguity and uncertainty. In place of such foundational concepts as objectivity and truth, postmodernists emphasize constructivism or perspectivism. And in contrast to the materialistic, isolated entity that characterizes the so-called modernist self, the postmodernist tends to see the self as generated and maintained by the relational, linguistic, and cultural contexts in which it is embedded.

The bifurcation of modernism and postmodernism is a reflection of changing theory and practice in contemporary psychoanalysis. Yet, any attempt to differentiate between varying perspectives inevitably raises certain questions.

A week After the horrific assault on the World Trade Center and Pentagon, a group of analysts gathered to support each other and share their impressions of how the events were affecting their patients and themselves. The material below consists of a partial sampling of some of the thoughts and clinical material raised during the meeting. The material is purposely being presented in relatively raw form. No attempt is made to construct an argument, draw generalizations, or theorize. Rather, we offer the readers a snapshot of what was foremost on the participants' minds during those dreadful days and the types of clinical encounters in which they were engaged. These are the highly individual yet overlapping voices of six clinicians who explicitly acknowledge that they cannot see the forest for the trees.

Dodi Goldman, Ph.D.

The attack on the World Trade Center was neither a disaster nor a tragedy. It was an atrocity perpetrated by fellow human beings who lived among their victims. The profound absence of empathy and the presence of deliberate intent to kill and be killed pose a challenge for which there is no obvious solution. The perpetrators were in no way cowards. They appear to have been men blinded by conviction.

Part of my initial reaction was a shameful thought. Before relocating to the U.S. in 1988, I lived in Israel on the Lebanese border. We had suffered a direct terrorist attack in 1979. Numerous additional attacks were thwarted. My children spent many nights in bomb shelters because of shelling from across the border. While in the army, my patrol jeep was ambushed. When I moved to the United States, I thought I had put all that behind.

Stanley Coen   training and supervising analyst, Columbia University Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research.

I Came to Psychoanalytic Training at the Columbia University Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research in 1968, already significantly influenced by the interpersonal tradition. As a psychiatric resident at the Henry Phipps Psychiatric Clinic of The Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore, much of what I was taught about the intensive therapy of more disturbed patients came from interpersonalists, especially Harry Stack Sullivan, Frieda Fromm-Rcichmann, Otto Will, Margaret and Janet Rioch, and many others. I was intrigued by the conferences I attended at Chestnut Lodge and seriously considered further training there, as had some of my colleagues. Alas, the United States Public Health Service (in Lexington, Kentucky), followed by my return to New York City, and psychoanalytic training intervened.

Of course, connections to White went back even further, to my reading Erich Fromm and Rollo May. As an undergraduate, I became very caught up in a paper I wrote on the possibility of being a “cheerful robot” for a course with C. Wright Mills. Fromm's (1941) Escape from Freedom had touched me deeply. I've just now made the connection between Fromm's writing and David Shapiro's (1981) Autonomy and Rigid Character, as focusing the wish to relinquish autonomy. I find this emphasis on surrendering autonomy very helpful in teaching candidates about obsessional and masochistic psychopathology, especially what it's like to analyze someone who doesn't want to feel and desire. And White had Fromm, May, Arieti, Schachtel, and others who loved to write, which I envied and wanted to emulate. When I was a psychiatric resident, because of his skill as a writer, Alan Wheelis was a hero of mine. As a writer, not as a psychoanalyst, Wheelis seemed like an interpersonal explorer. You may not realize that Baltimore analysts then did not write. They saw themselves as somewhat-Southern gentlemen (largely) who would reflect on the psychoanalytic literature evenings over cognac.

Cultures often have myths that define their origins and give meaning to their existence. The history of psychoanalysis is filled with such prized stories. Ruth Moulton, one of the first White Institute graduates, witnessed each step of the Institute's evolution out of schisms with the New York Psychoanalytic Institute and the group headed by Karen Horney. Her accounts of those events1 complement the histories written by Clara Thompson and Ralph Crowley. Taken together, these stories helped to create the persona that characterizes the White Institute as fiercely independent and fully committed to a vision of psychoanalytic possibility. It happens that this description is quite appropriate to Ruth herself.

As a young psychiatrist, recently relocated from the Midwest, Ruth Moulton began her training analysis with Clara Thompson in 1941 and was admitted to candidacy at the New York Psychoanalytic Institute. Her introduction to the psychoanalytic world was as an observer of the political struggle and intrigue that roiled the Institute later that same year. To recap those events briefly, in 1941 Karen Horney was a popular teacher at the New York Institute, although she was developing ideas that diverged from Freudian doctrine. The faculty, which consisted predominantly of male émigrés who had worked with Freud, voted to suspend Horney's teaching privileges. In a grand gesture, she left the meeting along with Clara Thompson, William Silverberg, and several others. In the famously repeated tale, the dissenters marched down Fifth Avenue, arm in arm, singing hymns of liberation. They, along with a number of their students and analysands, ceremoniously resigned from the Institute and formed a new training group under Horney's leadership. This new group, the American Institute of Psychoanalysis (AIP)

At a Time when our understanding of human experience has grown increasingly complex, and the awareness of cultural diversity is imperative to a clinician's unraveling this complexity, Jack Drescher presents us with an in-depth, readily accessible treatise on the unique conflicts that confront and often confuse gay men and their therapists.

More than forty years after Evelyn Hooker (1957) demonstrated that there are no differences between “homosexual” and “heterosexual” men, and almost thirty years since the APA removed homosexuality from the DSM, there still are psychoanalytic institutes in the world where homosexuality is pathologized. In fact, “for the third time, the International Psychoanalytical Association has…turned down a motion against discrimination based on sexual orientation” (Ubaldi, 2001). Drescher, however, informs us that things are changing. Gay and lesbian candidates are being accepted to psychoanalytic institutes where once they were shunned. Courageous people like Richard Isay (1989), Bert Schaffner (1996), and Drescher himself (1997) have opened the way for a paradigmatic shift in our thinking about normal gay development. They have demonstrated the usefulness of psychoanalytic inquiry (Sullivan, 1954) for the understanding of gay men and amelioration of suffering inherent in being born into a culture that appraises one as defective, abnormal, or sinful. Drescher has written a book in which he integrates two old adversaries: psychoanalytic theory and gay rights.

Drescher invites his readers to approach his book as if they were gay men themselves. He cautions us not to assume that we understand what it means or feels like to be gay, or that being gay means only one thing. Early in the book he makes the distinction between “homosexuality”—one aspect of a man's identity—and being gay. As analysts, we need always to be focused on the individual who comes to us presenting problems in living (Sullivan, 1953).

Joerg Bose MD

Joerg Bose

Joerg Bose   Director of the William Alanson White Institute; clinical assistant professor of psychiatry, Cornell University Medical College

Earl G. Witenberg, M.D., served as director of the William Alanson White Institute for thirty years, from 1963 to 1992. Dr. Witenberg's lengthy service, while extraordinary, was just one measure of his indefatigable and all-encompassing dedication to the White Institute. A larger-than-life personality, Earl's characteristic New England spareness, straightforwardness, stubbornness, and skepticism were well known and respected by his colleagues and his students. He was a compelling personality. Few people who came in contact with him left his presence without a story to tell.

Earl's scholarship was profound and his curiosity boundless. During his early tenure at the White Institute, his research vision encompassed a wide range of areas. He initiated a Visiting Distinguished Lecturer series and he spearheaded innovative conferences to which he invited scholars from many schools of thought. He intended their visits to enrich the Institute's intellectual foundation, and they did. Earl insisted on challenging conventional thinking and eschewing dogmatism, thereby contributing to the education and training of creative thinkers who could embrace ambiguity. Through his example, his scholarship, and his insistence on maintaining our uncertainty in the face of so many temptations to decide psychoanalytic questions once and for all, he made what may have been the crucial contribution to the essential and lasting identity of the White Institute.

Earl's pragmatism was nowhere more evident than in his leadership. He brought the White Institute from financial uncertainty to economic solvency, and it was his leadership and perspicacity that were responsible for the Institute's purchase of the landmark building it still occupies today. He felt that a psychoanalytic institute could not sustain itself unless it was constantly responsive to change. He was decisive: tough, persuasive, courageous, canny, and occasionally irascible.

Leon edel (1982) believed that artists often struggle with depression. He wrote of the aging Henry James, “In the ensuing five years we can read what seems to be characteristic of the history of every great artist—the moment when latent depression smothers the creative individual. In this crucible the artist faces the ultimate test: survive or go under” (p. 152).

The depressed writer has experience of great interest to the analyst. This Issue of Contemporary Psychoanalysis is dedicated to the memory of Ruth Moulton (1915-1999), who was so many things to the William Alanson White Institute. As Marylou Lionells tells us in the brief biographical essay that opens this collection of papers, Moulton was a loved and admired analyst, an inspiring supervisor and teacher, a dedicated administrator. Stanley Coen adds to this portrait in the course of telling us how Moulton, Alberta Szalita, and others, by participating in both the William Alanson White Institute and the Columbia University Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research, contributed to an “easy overlap” between these two institutions in the late 1960s and early 1970s and to an enduring mutual respect.

From the mid 1960s to the mid 1980s, when she was already well into middle age, Moulton published her ideas, quite often in this journal. What better way, then, to memorialize her in our pages than to examine the very topic she most often explored in those papers: the relationship of interpersonal psychoanalysis and feminism?

This issue of the journal is intended to be both a history of these issues and an update of them. Where have we been? Where are we now? Sue Shapiro contributes a long-needed, incisive, and fascinating history of the topic. Jane Flax evaluates in contemporary terms the work of Moulton, Clara Thompson, and Karen Horney, the people who, more than any others, formulated the beginnings of the relationship of interpersonal psychoanalysis and feminism. Edgar Levenson contributes some thoughts regarding Thompson, Moulton, and the evolution of interpersonal psychoanalysis. Michelle Price Miletic offers a review of Karen Horney's work on the psychology of women.

Recent and Current feminist discourses in psychoanalysis have shown a strong interest in the early writings of Karen Horney. In her time, Horney was a pioneer in two main areas: in the discipline that was then referred to as “feminine psychology,” and in the introduction of cultural factors to psychoanalytic theory. She was remarkable for her strong voice in challenging male-dominated theory, particularly in challenging Freud. This challenge was mounted in a variety of areas, including the origins of female sexuality, the dynamics of penis envy and the Oedipus complex, and the lack of emphasis and perceived degradation of motherhood within Freud's theories. Whereas the challenge to these particular points is essential to Horney's legacy and relevant to our current discourses regarding gender, perhaps more importantly it also reveals an underlying type of thinking that introduced social and political factors into the construction of theory and how women are viewed and regarded within it.

Horney was deeply influenced by sociology, particularly the work of Georg Simmel. She succeeded in introducing it into her own psychoanalytic lexicon, thereby allowing her to integrate intrapsychic and cultural contributions in her work. In essence, this served to deconstruct Freudian theory. Quite radically for the time, Horney exposed the biases and phallocentric views that contributed to the various theoretical suppositions of that era. She was able to articulate how it was in the male society's interest to accept and support particular views of women and their development. She proposed that the psychoanalytic theory of the day was driven by male reality and was not necessarily informed by girls' or women's experience of their femininity. Charles Strozier's biography is a rare and delightful surprise. Neither sanctimonious nor apologetic, the book is a welcome relief in the often fractious and ambitious world of psychoanalytic biographers since the days of Ernest Jones. Trained as a self psychologist, Strozier appreciates the developmental and therapeutic uses of idealization. As a biographer, however, he offers a rich and nuanced portrait of a complex man. For instance, Strozier acknowledges that much of his subject's writing is obtuse and jargon-laden, but never are the ideas themselves cast aside. Instead, the author systematically clarifies the body of Kohut's work, taking us on a developmental journey. At first the gifted, charismatic, narcissistically vulnerable Heinz embraces orthodoxy. As he ages and sickens, he breaks out of the mold with the support of a fawning group of talented, but younger, impressionable colleagues. Ultimately a national movement is formed in which identity and empathy are placed on par with conflict and interpretation, forever altering the theory and technique of psychoanalysis.

Strozier toiled at least twenty years on this project, taking time to interview family, patients, colleagues, and friends, and waiting for Kohut's correspondence to be released in 1994. The resulting volume is packed with evocative tidbits that only intimates would know. We receive an affecting picture of Kohut's own noisy grandiosity when he insists on sitting naked in his hospital bed long after a favorite nurse bathed and powdered him. Other medical personnel refuse to enter his room and call him a “pervert,” (p. 323), but this does not deter a delighted Kohut from his show.

The Irrationality of massive destruction and homicide throws us into mistrust. After World War I, in his wish to understand the irrationality of mass behavior and his hunger for peace and mutual understanding in the international community, Erich Fromm (1962) made it his rule to “doubt everything.” However accustomed one may be to lonely voyages in the sea of the unconscious, one is never free from doubt. To use an ancient metaphor for the world, the direction that the huge turtle is heading can hardly be known to those of us living on the turtle's back (Levenson, 1972).

The difference for modern society is that we see catastrophe with our own eyes, using communication technology and media networks. Fifty years ago, most Japanese didn't know what had happened in Hiroshima, even well after the war ended. Now most of them could watch the collapse of the World Trade Center in real time. We live at a historical moment when heads of government apologize to citizens for being unable to provide real-time coverage of a war.

Has any of this increased our sense of where the world is headed? Unfortunately, it doesn't seem to be the case. When I returned to Japan in November 2001, I was surprised that TV news and other programs were covering the everyday life of ordinary Afghans—something I had rarely seen in New York. After the Mass Murders of September 11, 2001, in New York, Washington, and Pennsylvania, and with the subsequent terror created by anthrax in the mail, Americans came to identify themselves as under attack, under threat of further attack, and as survivors of attack. Since Pearl Harbor, the entire population has not felt so threatened in its own territory. Yet there are neighborhoods in the United States whose

residents live with violence on a daily basis, such as sections of inner cities with high crime rates. There are first-generation immigrants who come from countries with recent or longstanding histories of war and communal violence, immigrants whose memories and experiences continue to haunt them in this country. There are also survivors of natural disasters, airplane crashes, terrorist acts by fringe groups, and murders perpetrated on groups of people by psychopaths, cult members, and even by the government of the United States itself (as in Waco, Texas). Identification with the victims and survivors of September 11 extended the occasional, local, or particular experience of violence and living through violence to a national scale.

With a renewed interest forced upon us, then, I review a book published several years ago on the suffering and healing of youth living through war and communal violence. The editors of Minefields in Their Hearts are psychiatrist-psychoanalysts affiliated with Harvard Medical School and the Boston Psychoanalytic Institute. This volume of twelve chapters is the outcome of a project undertaken by the Children in War and Communal Violence International Working Group (an affiliate of the International Association of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Allied Professionals). The editors state their belief that psychologically informed interventions can ameliorate the injury caused to children by war and communal violence. They also believe that those who work with these children must develop an active commitment to try to change conditions that allow such violence.

Helen Swick Perry, editor, researcher, and author, died July 26 at age ninety. She was hired by Harry Stack Sullivan in 1946 to assist with the enthusiastic response to the second series of William Alanson White Memorial Lectures (presented by Brock Chisholm). She became managing editor later that year, a post she held until 1955, when work on the posthumous series of Sullivan books precluded an ongoing commitment to Psychiatry. Helen built the journal in to a self-sustaining enterprise, evident in a tripling of subscriptions and manuscript submissions.

She is also widely respected for her definitive biography of Sullivan, Psychiatrist of America (1982), and for her matchless work with the posthumous Sullivan book series.

She was a gifted author who used Sullivan's interpersonal approach to acquire new insights into social phenomena. Her 1954 Psychiatry paper was the first to apply the concept of selective inattention to international relations. (“Selective Inattention as an Explanatory Concept for U.S. Public Attitudes Toward the Bomb”). While doing research at Langley Porter Neuro-Psychiatric Institute she spent time as a participant-observer, analyzing the newly emerging “hippie” movement. The Human Be-In (1970) is still a highly regarded portrait of Haight-Ashbury. Her optimistic appraisal met something of the same star-crossed fate as the topic she addressed. The book release party coincided with the killings at Kent and Jackson State, a pivotal moment when peace and love were rapidly deteriorating into despair and hedonism.

During the Second World War, she was a writer for the War Production Board. She also worked for the Child Research branch of NIH in the 1950s and pursued research at the Massachusetts Mental Health Center (Boston). She was a graduate of George Washington University and the recipient of a certificate in Applied Psychology from the Washington School of Psychiatry. She was an honorary member of the Harry Stack Sullivan Society of the William Alanson White Institute. She taught at the University of California Medical School (San Francisco).

Are Women deficient men? Karen Horney, Clara Thompson, and Ruth Moulton believed that the psychoanalytic theories dominant in their time consigned women to this position. To counter the deficiency model, Horney, Thompson, and Moulton propose substituting a positive account of “true womanhood.” Rather than accepting the male as the norm, they suggest creating two separate but equal normative standards. Woman's true nature could only be revealed and affirmed when she is defined and analyzed by the unique categories appropriate to her. Although nuances vary in their constitution of true womanhood, the approaches of these analysts overlap. Several binaries ground and shape their shared beliefs. These include nature-culture, biology-psychology, men-women, masculinity-femininity, and heterosexual-homosexual. Within this frame, each writer struggles against the devaluation of, and contempt for, women that remains all too prevalent today. They fruitfully open up psychoanalytic discourse to consideration of the influences of social contexts and power relations on its own ideas. Yet, by constructing their accounts through these polarities and accepting conventional ideas of the meaning of most, their alternative results in naturalizing gender and thereby imprisoning woman within its constraints. In her writings, each theorist also undercuts some of the most radical insights of psychoanalysis, including the contingency and fragility of gender arrangements, the complexity of psychic representation, the social construction of sexualities, and the hybrid qualities of psychic-somatic processes.

The work of each of these authors can be read as cautionary tales concerning the costs of theoretical strategies and the power of regressive forces within sites of analytic concern. They direct our attention to the importance and difficulties of resisting normative social constructions that are deeply invested by and with intrapsychic and social power.

Psychoanalysts feel a sense of purpose now, maybe even especially now. We know, and we see and feel every day, that what we do is at the center of the lives of those with whom we do it. So many of the sessions that have taken place since September 11 have been directly or indirectly shaped by the events of that date. Even when we and our patients are not thinking explicitly about the new dangers, the context of our lives has changed. A new sense of threat and precariousness dwells within us. There is at least a silent nuance of September 11 with us all the time. But in this changed world, we know, beyond the shadow of a doubt, that what we do matters. We can see every day that the work to which we devote ourselves contributes to the lives around us, and thus to our own.

And yet, of course, we hope to offer something more than comfort. Just as we did before September 11, we hope to offer the opportunity for greater freedom. Years ago we were readier than we are now to conceive difficulties in living as neurosis, and to imagine that when neurosis was “resolved” (so the story went) the blinders would fall from the patient's eyes and the “entire view” would be there to see. In the postmodern world of the present day, we can no longer believe we know what that “entire view” is. We are now much more willing to take the position that any views—not only the views of an individual, but the views available within any culture—are a selection of the possibilities, a construction of experience that might have been constructed otherwise. For some time now we have not been able to accept that we merely uncover what we find in psychoanalysis; we participate in constructing it. We do not merely reveal; we influence. We work toward an awareness of the nature of that influence, but we know we can never grasp it all. Some of it we have no choice but to live out; some of it, in fact, we now recognize as mutative.

In Recent Years there has been a growing body of memoir written by those suffering from depression about their experience of illness and treatment. Among the many noteworthy contributions to this literature are William Styron's (1990) Darkness Visible: A Memoir of Madness; Kay Redfield Jamison's (1996) An Unquiet Mind; Jeffery Smith's (1999) Where the Roots Reach for Water: A Personal and Natural History of Melancholia; and Nell Casey's (2001) edited collection of short pieces, Unholy Ghost: Writers on Depression. Andrew Solomon made an initial contribution to this literary evocation of suffering in a 1998 New Yorker piece, a contribution that he has extended in his remarkable book, The Noonday Demon: An Atlas of Depression. The book is at once a harrowing personal account of his own relentless struggle with treatment-resistant depression, a far-reaching venture into cross-cultural field research, a scholarly, if at times somewhat tendentious, review of all aspects of the clinical literature on depression and related topics, and a meditation on the nature and meaning of suffering in our lives.

The chapter headings, Depression, Breakdowns, Treatments, Alternatives, Populations, Addiction, Suicide, History, Poverty, Evolution, and Hope, convey the breadth of Solomon's ambition, an ambition realized with varying degrees of success for each of these subjects. The Noonday Demon is strongest when Solomon stays close to his own experience and that of the many resilient men and women who entrusted their stories to him.

Every vocational career has its limitations and its own particular perils. For us as analytic practitioners, boredom is one of the most ubiquitous and untoward. Yet, the vast volume of material examining clinical practice has largely ignored boredom. Those who write about psychoanalysis appear to have made the tacit assumption that once an analyst has acquired clinical skills, he or she should be able to remain attentive and curious over a lifetime of practice. Those who have made this judgment have poorly served their colleagues. Severe ennui seriously afflicts a considerable number of practitioners, if not every analyst at some point in a full-time practice.

In that people who are drawn to practicing psychoanalysis are generally highly stimulated by and responsive to the inner life, a state of boredom stands in sharp contrast to their usual way of being-in-the-world. It usually indicates that they have lost touch with the goals, purposes, and directions with which they entered their career, such as gaining important realizations about oneself by learning from clients. We Take it for Granted that psychoanalysis can inform our understanding of the human condition of hatred. But through understanding our experiences of hating and being hated, can we also inform psychoanalytic theory and its application?

I take it to be a basic truth that everyone has experienced hating and being hated. Hatred is an ordinary human experience that has extraordinary results. Maybe it is because of those extraordinary outcomes that we accord hatred the status of taboo. We seem to feel, in the common culture, that if we speak hate's name or invoke its memory we will suffer a grim consequence. On the other hand, we fantasize that if we don't speak it, it doesn't exist. The collusion of silence makes hatred unbearably dangerous.

I think that all of us have our hate-stories to tell, if we dare. We all have our hate-scars, some of which are better healed than others, and some of us are better healed, as persons who have hated and been hated, than others.

So I accept not only that our theory teaches us about hate, but also that, if we converse with one another about our experiences of hatred, we may demystify it, and that may allow us to inform and enliven psychoanalytic theory about hatred, and may even ameliorate the effects of hating and being hated within ourselves. We would undertake this piece of work on behalf of our own personal and professional development, as well as on behalf of our patients, In a small way, we would also undertake it on behalf of the global community, where the monstrous results of hatred proliferate.

I have had many kinds of conversations about hating and being hated. Some go this way: “Those hateful things are in the past. Things are different, now.”

During the Summer of my daughter's second year, when talking was at best a jumble of kaleidoscopic images, loosely organized containers of experience, book-ended by action and tears, a repetitive refrain emerged for weeks on end: “I want to go home …”

No matter where we were, “home” or not, the refrain continued. Home remained an elusive place of striving, ever unattainable.

Quickly falling into an abyss of rational reasoning that is so often the thwarted goal with two year olds, I found myself wondering what it felt like to “want to go home.” I found myself thinking that perhaps this was indeed a rich and contained means of verbalizing the concept of wanting in general. I also was aware that our beloved nanny was overseas for a month and “home” may have had something to do with this temporary loss. Questioning this with my daughter, the wanting seemed to be given form and shape. Soon enough, “I want to go home” was transformed into “I want Tanya.”

I initially delighted in my ability to allow my child access to the world of words as a means of communicating her inner experience. Yet questions (no doubt permeating my world from constant exposure to postmodern thinking) remained. While seemingly unleashing my daughter's experience, had I also curtailed or deflected it? My daughter was hardly unaware of my pleasure in this whole interaction. She would now laughingly say “I want Tanya” and look to me for my reaction. What she had originally “wanted” was now complicated by a charged and loving exchange. What was it that she wanted? And was she indeed now “home”?

In Need of Wanting

“Home” for Moulton was a complicated affair. This was as much a place of safety as it was a capricious base from which messages about independence and success waffled at best.

The Term “implicit communication” emerged from cognitive psychology, and has entered psychoanalytic discourse via infancy research. In these contexts, “explicit” communication refers, for the most part, to verbal communication and to messages that we intend to transmit and that we know consciously we are transmitting. “Implicit” communication refers to the nonverbal levels of communication, to messages that we are transmitting automatically or without conscious intent or even conscious knowledge. The broadest modality of implicit communication is action patterns, and more specifically facial expression, posture and movement patterns, and the prosodic and rhythmic levels of vocalization. Implicit communication is thought to operate outside conscious awareness in the cognitive sense.1 Analysts might well suspect that implicit channels carry information that is repressed or dissociated as well. Related concepts in this domain are “procedural knowledge,” that is, things we know how to do automatically, like walk or conduct a conversation with another person, and “declarative knowledge,” that is, things we know in words or as facts, as in the content of statements. Cognitive psychologists believe that all communications have both levels, implicit and explicit, so that the recipient of a communication is receiving multiple messages on conscious and unconscious levels.

For the Past Fifteen Years, the analytic literature has been dominated by the intersubjective, interpersonal, and relational approaches. Reacting to the reign of positivistic, authoritarian, ill-conceived notions of the analyst as all-knowing, perfectly analyzed, and neutral, what has become known as the one-person perspective has been effectively set aside as a viable model. Or has it? While most people seem to agree with the basic relational and intersubjective approaches outlined by Aron, Benjamin, Ghent, Hirsch, Levenson, Mitchell, Stolorow, and innumerable colleagues, many people have balked at both the theory and potential applications of social construction. The constructivist model began with Hoffman's (1983) classic paper, “The Patient as Interpreter of the Analyst's Experience,” and most clinicians read it with relief. Much of the literature that followed informed clinicians of the subjective nature of the analytic relationship—something they already knew from their own clinical experience.

Finally, all the things we were actually experiencing with patients were being said out loud. We were off the hook for not being perfect. And we were freed from trying to practice in ways that did not work very well. We could stop being authoritarian, rude, and withholding. We could be human beings and analysts at the same time. This trend toward humanizing the analytic process and acknowledging the inherent mutuality seemed unstoppable.

This Commemorative Issue seems an appropriate place to review some aspects of the evolution of interpersonal psychoanalysis since my first meeting with Ruth Moulton in 1951, when I applied for candidacy to the William Alanson White Institute. It is, of course, a personal and impressionistic version with which surely not everyone will agree.

She had, I knew, a reputation as an “analyst's analyst,” especially for women. She was a great favorite of bright, young, educated women—analysts, professional women of all ilk, housewives, other analysts' wives and girlfriends. She was writing extensively about women's problems; to be an interpersonalist was, as I elaborate, pari passu, to be a feminist. But potential patients select analysts less for their prominence or reputation and rather more because they see the analyst as a role model: someone they feel had faced and successfully dealt with their kind of problems. She overwhelmingly met these criteria. She was married to an analytic colleague, had handsome and accomplished children from two marriages, wrote and taught extensively, lived a sophisticated, intellectual life. Also, she'd had the courage to leave her candidacy at the New York Psychoanalytic Institute and follow her analyst, Clara Thompson, and Erich Fromm into exile. And as I discovered in my interview with her—and I can't remember how I learned this—she was a great admirer of the modernist and protofeminist, Virginia Woolf. Perhaps it's inconsequential, but she was, like the young Virginia Woolf, serenely beautiful.

Recently my father told me about the great deal he'd gotten on some polo shirts: $4.99, marked down from $25. He said, “It was at a store that sells sportswear, called Joe … no, it was Joe's … Joe's.…” He trailed off, frowning and pursing his lips with the frustration of not remembering. Without thinking twice, I said, “Eddie Bauer?” He looked a little startled. “How did you know that?”

I didn't know how I knew. But that wasn't the first time.

Twenty years ago, I had a dream about my father. He was lying with his eyes closed in a hospital bed, and behind him, on the wall, was a thing like a thermometer that I understood to be a blood pressure monitor. The blood-red fluid in the monitor began to rise. It rose higher and higher until the top of the glass that held it shattered and it spewed out into the air. I awoke terrified, breathing hard, with the strongest kind of feeling—I would say “knowledge,” actually, though I was reluctant to say that at the moment, there in my bed in the middle of the night—that my father, who had high blood pressure and various other cardiac risk factors, had had a heart attack. Early the next morning I told my analyst the dream and we analyzed it. When I returned home from analysis I received a call from my mother, telling me that my father had had chest pains the previous night and that he had gone to the hospital, where the diagnosis of a heart attack had just been made. I might have suspected myself of secondary revision if I had not already told my analyst the dream.

I am fairly hardheaded about matters such as these. I am impatient with credulous accounts of preknowledge, clairvoyance, thought transmission, and so on. And yet I cannot ignore what happened to me.

To seek reality is both to set out to explore the injury inflicted by it, to turn back on, and to try to penetrate, the state of being stricken, wounded by reality,—and to attempt, at the same time to reemerge from the paralysis of this state, to engage reality, as an advent, a movement, and as a vital critical necessity of moving on.

—S. Felman and D. Laub, 1992

In an earlier article (Boulanger, 2002), I described a forty-one-year-old businessman, Jonah, who was referred for treatment eighteen months after having been violently assaulted for no apparent reason by a battery of policemen in the hallway of his apartment building. Throughout the assault, he'd feared that at any moment he would be killed. This chance encounter left him in a posttraumatic no-man's-land. “I keep seeing these things over and over again,” he told me. “They just come into my mind … I can't cast a shadow over them. Time has gone. I am in a dead end. It's like you are walking along and suddenly you hit a wall. You can't go back and you can't go forward, you keep hitting the wall. I used to be interested in what was going on. Now I don't go out. I don't read the paper in case I read of violence. I don't watch television … I have lost hope of things being different … I am emotionally devastated … I have lost my soul.”

Jonah's symptoms are typical of the posttraumatic state: intrusive memories of the beating and consequent avoidance of anything that might remind him of it; the disruption of his sense of time and of his interpersonal relationships; feelings of numbness and loss of interest in the world around him.

The analyst feels not only the patient, but also himself in seeking to discover his own humanity in the other, in experiencing the universal human in himself and in the other.

Biancoli, 2002

Experiencing the universally human is a potential source of joy in analysis. It is available to both participants. My response to Biancoli's essay is to explore the nature of this, and other sources of joy that I believe are at the heart of the analytic encounter.

Focusing on our common humanity can promote the sense that we can transcend our particular idiosyncrasies and circumstances and that can bring us joy. But there is a second fundamental source of joy in analysis, in the process of defining and affirming our unique individuality. Biancoli writes of analysis as “a dialogue between analyst and analysand aimed at clarifying who the latter is and why he is the way he is, that is to say, at unsticking his process of individuation.” (p. 609). Biancoli goes on to describe how “the analyst's own process of individuation is also activated.”

Thus I am differentiating two fundamental opportunities for joy in the treatment process. These two joys, the joy of affirming uniqueness and the joy of transcending it, can hearten both analyst and patient. Both, I believe, fortify the relationship, allowing it to weather its inevitable challenges. Despite difficulties, a treatment can survive and its participants thrive if there is sufficient joy.

I begin by exploring the nature of joy. First, I compare Fromm's and Schachtel's conceptions of joy with concepts drawn from emotion theory and the poetry of Wordsworth. Then, moving to the analytic encounter, I explore some of its potential joys. In a final section I reframe these sources of joy, in a further effort to clarify just what each celebrates.

The Game of Baseball has some interesting areas of overlap with psychoanalysis and psychoanalytic psychotherapy. For example, sporting enthusiasts tell us that one of the hardest things to do in sports is the act of hitting a baseball. The act of striking a small spherical object moving at a high rate of speed with a cylindrical object is exceedingly difficult by itself. But that's only the beginning. The amount of time it takes a 90 mph fastball to leave the pitcher's hand and arrive in the catcher's glove is .41 seconds. It takes approximately .28 seconds to initiate and complete a full swing of the bat. This leaves the batter about .13 seconds to determine whether or not he likes the pitch, decide to swing at it or not, and then where to swing the bat. Moreover, if the batter's swing is .03 seconds off in either direction (i.e., being ahead or behind the pitch), he will miss the ball entirely. If the quartzlike precision in timing involved in hitting a ball were not difficult enough, there are also 13 points of movement in the human body involved in the motion of swinging a bat, all of which have to be perfectly coordinated in order to make contact with the ball, much less hit it well enough to get on base. As the batter performs the motion of swinging a bat to hit the ball, he cannot focus conscious attention on what his body is doing, for such concentrated awareness would seriously interfere with his task and likely cause him to distort his swing in a way that would make him miss the ball. He must, in other words, perform his skill in a state of relative unconsciousness.

Needless to say, hitting a baseball is a very complex process that requires a great deal of skill, training, and practice. In this article, I explore how our work as analytic therapists might be similar to the batter's task in complexity, timing, and unconscious action.

The Field of psychoanalysis has become increasingly feminized. With few exceptions, however, men still hold most of the power, charisma, and influence in the field. When I came to the White Institute for training I selected a man for my training analysis. Most of the analytic supervisors I chose were also men. In this essay I discuss an experience that helped me to mobilize and express power and assertiveness that did not occur in my analysis or with my male supervisors, although both were important background figures. The experience occurred, instead, with a female patient who was uncomfortable with her aggression and assertiveness. She noted my discomfort with my own aggression and attacked me in various ways for not being a powerful male analyst and for being too similar and equal to her. In the course of these attacks I became able to recognize my own aggression and assertiveness. Coming to terms with the aggression in our relationship invigorated the analysis and engendered power and assertiveness in both the patient and me.

Winnicott (1949) writes, “There are many patients who need us to be able to give them a capacity to use us. This for them is the analytic task.” The analyst must demonstrate his or her ability to survive the patient's destructiveness in order to become a separate person to the patient. There are certain patients who make it difficult for a particular analyst to tolerate and survive their destructiveness. Contempt and denigration by a female patient can be especially difficult for a female analyst to tolerate. When the analyst herself is lacking in a secure sense of power and influence, such contempt and denigration from a female patient can activate feelings of helpless rage in the analyst that can render her paralyzed and unable to think and function. Thus the analyst becomes impotent and is of no use to the patient.

What psychoanalysts do is more a function of each uniquely individual analyst than theoretical allegiance per se. Nonetheless, the latter also normally has considerable significance. These conceptually based community ties (Aron, 1996; Greenberg, 1999) are often most evident around questions and controversies concerning the relative significance of interpretation in effecting mutative action. They also appear when we observe the contents of interpretations and how these commonly fall into clusters that are based on analysts' “school” or tradition. Sandler (1983), however, astutely observes that no one actually knows what analysts do behind closed doors. What is usually described in the literature is what we want our respective communities of cotheorists to know about us, and this normally conforms to “family” values. Sandler also suggests that analysts have what he calls “private theories” that are not necessarily in harmony with publicly shared ones. These private activities and theories coordinate with therapeutic interventions that may bear only marginal resemblance to written or oral reports in journals and conferences. With this caveat in mind I briefly trace the history of the community of interpersonal psychoanalysis and its intersection with the newer and broader designation, the relational perspective The analytic activities of these traditions, interpretation and beyond, are well characterized by Hoffman's (1998) discussions of spontaneity, or “throwing away the book,” while still adhering to psychoanalytic ritual, or “the book.”

*A variation of this paper was presented at the PEP CD-ROM-sponsored Symposium 2001; What Psychoanalysts Do: Interpretation and Beyond, New York, N.Y., February, 2001. The key questions posed to all panelists (representing a range of theoretical traditions) were: (1) How significant a role does interpretation play in your analytic activity? (2) What else do you do in addition to interpretation? The primary interest of the conference organizers was to clarify whether analysts still view interpretation as the central vehicle of analysts' participation, and what other modes of analytic participation may have replaced or now accompany interpretive activity. The variant presented here is an effort to address these questions from an interpersonal-relational perspective.

He helped all of us on the Board to become better editors. I am very pleased that all the members of the Board of those years will stay on, and that those who I have asked to join the Board have agreed to serve.

In Nocturnes: On Listening to Dreams, Paul Lippmann expresses deep concern over the impact of modern cyber-culture on privacy, imagination, and dream life. In Lippmann's view, the rapid proliferation of electronic technology and scientific knowledge, as well as excessive access to external stimulation and passive entertainment, has lead to a loss of contact with the private moment and the self-generative aspects of solitude and self-reflection. Modern times have literally squeezed the soul out of much of inner life. Lippmann believes we are less able to maintain a private world, due to the power and reach of the global market and mass media that shape our thoughts, imaginations, and desires. For him, the dreaming mind is the last safe haven for private experience in the twenty-first century.

Lippmann criticizes both classical Freudian and relational psychoanalysts as contributing to a recent decreased interest in dreams and disconnection of soul from nature by crowding dreams into specific interpretative architectures. ‘In his view, the Freudian mistrust of latent content, emphasis on depth interpretations, and rigid adherence to fixed interpretations of universal symbols has stifled the inherent freedom of dreams to teach and guide. Lippmann views modern relational analysts as preoccupied with seeing reflections of themselves in their patients’ dreams.

To counterbalance these trends, he advocates a particular attitude and sensibility when approaching dreams. His refreshingly naturalistic-interpersonal perspective includes a deep respect and appreciation for the mystery and creative power of the unconscious.

I have two Memories of Ruth Moulton. These memories, spanning twenty years, say as much about me, my sense of changes in the culture, and the status of women as they do about Ruth Moulton.1 As such, they also provide my own starting point for this essay—an inquiry into the evolution of feminist interpersonal psychoanalytic theory and theorists.

My first memory is not of a specific moment, but of a cluster of impressions of Dr. Moulton seen from afar in the early 1970s at the William Alanson White Institute. I was a graduate student at the time and would anxiously frequent the Friday night colloquia at the Institute. I always felt a bit out of place then, self-conscious and in awe of the “real,” “grown up” analysts who might one day have a say in my future. There weren't many women faculty and supervisors then, although there were certainly more professional women than I was used to seeing collected in one place. I was especially conscious of the women as I scanned the room in search of role models: Anna Antonovsky, Marianne Eckardt, Geneva Goodrich, Anna Gourevich, Janet Jeppson, Ruth Moulton, Natalie Shainess, Rose Spiegel, Alberta Szalita, Ann Ruth Turkel; and from the next generation, Leah Davidson, Harrict Field, Gloria Friedman, Elaine Grimm, Roberta Held-Weiss, Helene Kafka, Marylou Lionells, Carola Mann, Marcia Rosen, Anita Tenzer, Hazel Weinberg. My search was accompanied by a fear that these “real” women might recognize me as an impostor, a girl (cf. Dinnerstein, 1976; Riviere, 1927; Horner, 1972; Horner & Walsh, 1974; Symonds, 1971). I believed that these older female analysts would not be taken in by me, that they could see through me.

Whom is it possible to analyze? It used to be traditional for psychoanalytic institutes to have a course in analyzability. While many institutes today do not have such a course, others still do. Even in many of the institutes that do not have such a course, the question is still considered seriously, but often inadequately. The question is usually formulated in terms of there being certain patients who are analyzable and certain patients who are not analyzable. In essence, the question is whether the patient is good enough to be analyzed; that is, whether the patient has a high level of ego functioning and object relations, which will make a therapeutic alliance easy to achieve, and a full transference neurosis easy to develop, easily tolerated, and easily resolved. A great deal of thought has gone into what aspects of ego functioning are most relevant and how best to measure them. On the other hand, history shows how vain this search is.

It is the wrong question. The right question is, What needs to be done to make this person an analyzable patient?

The problem of the analyzable patient is not just a problem for institutes and training. Today we hear analysts decrying the absence of suitable patients. You cannot make a living as a psychoanalyst; there are just too many psychoanalysts and not enough psychoanalytic patients. And if, by “suitable patient,” you mean someone who does not have serious problems, has no serious ego deficits or characterological problems, makes no phone calls, has no emergencies or unexpected crises, comes in four or five times a week, and pays a large fee, indeed there may very well be few analyzable patients.

But if a suitable patient is someone who is hurting badly and is willing to work because he or she is desperate, who may have to be seen on a sliding scale, who has crises and provides challenges, then there are patients, and they are interesting, treatable patients.

Two people together is a work

Heroic in it's ordinariness.

The slow-picked, halting traverse of a pitch

Where the fiercest attention becomes routine…

—Adrienne Rich

Imagine a bespectacled Harry Stack Sullivan in a depression-era bowtie, listening with the intensity I always imagine he listened with, sitting on a panel with contemporary feminist psychoanalysts—Nancy Chodorow and Jessica Benjamin, for instance. Raised by his grandmother, mother, and aunt, away from his emotionally remote father and the “manly” outdoor farm chores, Harry would sit around the farmhouse table with the women and talk about books and ideas (Perry, 1982). Sullivan probably worried about being called a sissy because he didn't take on the male role at home or at school. I imagine him welcoming his feminist colleagues and their more prismatic notions of gender and relatedness as light through a gray rural sky. As those who knew him professionally tell us (Perry, 1984; White, 1978), he was capable not only of the scientific aloofness that so often characterized men of his professional and societal rank, but also of a highly attuned tenderness. Such was Sullivan's demeanor toward those patients most fragile and disenfranchised, those likely to expect dismissal to the proverbial bottom of the barrel (White, 1978). Many of his friends were women. He encouraged one of them, Clara Thompson, to pursue a training analysis with Sandor Ferenczi, after hearing Ferenczi speak of the importance of a more mutual tie between patient and therapist.

A Patient describes a recent conversation with his father. Once again, the patient is invited to join his father in financially providing extra resources for his younger siblings. Although the patient can afford to do this presently, the future looks extremely uncertain in his field. Of late, he has spoken often of his anxiety about his own financial security.

The patient recounts how he quickly agreed to help his siblings, so they would have the “peace of mind” of “extra reserves.” Then he becomes noticeably uninterested in going over the details of the plan with his father, and equally uninterested in exploring it in treatment. His summary, in a nonchalant voice, is a repetition of the word “whatever.” It wasn't that important.

The feeling I had was that this was a “fait accompli.” I wasn't, to question his acceding to the request. I wasn't to react as though this had much significance. I was merely to notice how his father assumed the patient hadn't needs of his own. Just as the patient was expected to unresistantly pay, I was expected to unresistantly accept he had no choice other than to go along with his father's plan.

What does this patient need most from me? Who must I be to help him? Can I be any competent analyst (harkening back to classical thinking, e.g., Freud, 1912)? Can I be any trained analyst able to “handle” her countertransference so it doesn't “disrupt” the process? Or are there human qualities, aside from technical competence, that are crucial to effective work with this patient?

In this clinical situation, I believe an important variable is my stance toward certain specific challenges in life. In what follows I claborate some aspects of my own development as a person that I think are relevant to my treatment of this patient.

Ghislaine Boulanger   teaching and supervisory faculty, Clinical Psychology Program, Teachers College, Columbia University.

The Two Essays that follow were written in another era. It was an era before the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001 made the cost of physical and psychological survival of immediate concern to all of us in New York and in Washington, if not in America and in the rest of the world. The first of these articles explores the epistemological muddle that psychoanalysts can get into when they try to account for long-term reactions to massive psychic trauma. The second article proposes a way out of this muddle.

In the immediate aftermath of the terrorist attacks, I asked myself if these papers were still relevant. Mental health professionals generally, among them many psychoanalysts, have risen magnificently to the overwhelming need to offer support to survivors, the families of the missing, and relief workers. In New York, there are constant appeals for mental health volunteers to meet with families as they search hospital records for missing relatives. Licensed professionals are sought to support husbands, wives, children, and parents as they come to terms with the fact that there will never be a body to bury, that only a death certificate will bring some type of closure to this period uncertainty. Volunteers speak with fire fighters or police or medical examiners weighed down by their personal losses and the grisly tasks they are being asked to perform. Other professionals have been invited to debrief corporations, trying to get on with business as usual, where managers and workers alike fear the world will never be usual again. The requests for volunteers are filled almost as soon as they appear on the different listserves and telephone trees to which we all subscribe. And all this painful work comes on top of the ongoing treatment of our regular patients, some of whom have already experienced other more private catastrophes in their own lives. For them, the analytic work has taken on new urgency.

In this Article, I examine certain aspects of the relationship between the process of individuation and the analytic work. I begin with a commitment to the idea that the process of individuation is central. The viewpoint from which I set out is that of Erich Fromm's radical humanism.

I encounter various problems in the course of my inquiry. Some of these, including transference, countertransference, and relativism versus a belief in universal aspects of human nature, I take as themes to be investigated in turn in the humanist perspective. To clarify the viewpoint adopted here it is not always enough to set forth Fromm's thought. Sometimes it needs to be explicated, if not indeed interpreted.

I believe I must present here, preliminarily, a theoretic question regarding the general framing of Frommian psychoanalytic thought. Fromm says that he is “like a pupil and translator of Freud” (Evans, 1966, p. 59). In The Legacy of Erich Fromm, Daniel Burston (1991) classifies psychoanalysts in three groups, depending on their relationship to Freud: “loyal opposition,” “dissident fringe,” and “cryptorevisionists.” He places Fromm in the loyal opposition, together with Groddeck, Ferenczi, Karen Horney (in her early writings), Fairbairn, Guntrip, and others.

In an interview with Evans (1966) and in The Crisis of Psychoanalysis (1970), Fromm declares his links of friendship and collaboration with Karen Horney, Clara Thompson, and Harry Stack Sullivan, but is careful to distinguish his theoretic positions from those of his friends. ONE OF THE THINGS that delights me about Donnel Stern's discussion of my paper is that it expands our sense of mystery. He states: “We know no more about where our everyday, unremarkable, reflective experience comes from than we do where thought transmission or clairvoyance does.” This sentence, at once astonishing and obvious, recaptures a sense of wonder in the workings of the mind, something we usually take for granted. And then further on: “The obdurate strangeness of dreams has always been reassuring to us.” At first, I hesitated before this statement, remembering the multitude of times I struggled to find THE meaning, any meaning, in a dream in order to justify my claim to expertise. At those times, I felt far from reassured. But then, he goes on, “it shows us that the mystery of experience survives all our interpretations, preserving the possibility of meaningful futures we never know to expect.” Our focus is shifted to those times when we thought we had an interpretation of a dream, when we thought we had our hands around the elusive wild thing. It slithers out of our grasp, as long as we don't turn dogmatic, ending the inquiry. But then Stern makes another astonishing leap: he reminds us that the “obdurate strangeness” of dreams preserves “the possibility of meaningful futures we never knew to expect.” The very potential of psychoanalysis to transform a life depends on the continually regenerating elusiveness of experiencel This line of thinking reminds me why psychoanalysis (and Eastern spiritual traditions) appealed to me in the first place. Way back in high school and college I was fascinated with inklings and intimations, with the sense of transcendent significances just beyond the horizon. Stern's writing stimulates that sense of wonder, as does some of the recent psychoanalytic writing that brings together psychoanalysis and nonlinear dynamic systems theory (e.g., Sander, 2002; Ghent, in press). When this latter writing points to the “self-organizing” properties of dynamic systems, to “emergent” organizations, it points toward that irreducible mystery of where our “everyday, unremarkable, reflective experience comes from.

In Recent Years, much of my interest has been on what knowledge of the Holocaust and Holocaust studies stirs in the witness and bystander (Prince, 1985a, 1998). I do not believe that it is possible to think meaningfully about the Holocaust without self-examination. In his assault on my book, Alan Grey admonishes me for my “idiosyncratic biases.” Grey might have done well to consider some of his own “idiosyncratic biases” in deciding to review my book, as well as his reading of it. To begin with, Grey should have disclosed the unpleasant personal relationship between us that might have had a bearing on his decision to review the book and his reaction to it. More importantly, he could have tried to reflect on his own attitudes about the Holocaust that are portrayed throughout the review. Had he done so, perhaps he could have permitted reasonable consideration of important issues, rather than produce a distorted picture. In his characterization of the book, Grey misreads, misunderstands, misrepresents, selectively attends, and quotes out of context. His review betrays a lack of understanding of the book's approach, what it presents as findings, and, most importantly, about the Holocaust itself. It may have significance, however, as an example of the reactions the Holocaust elicits.

The underlying assumption of Legacy, the context in which the children of survivors were studied, is that the Holocaust was a historical event of massive significance, one that defined the twentieth century and fully justified the historian George Kren's (1980, 1984) characterization of it as a “historical novum.” As Marcus and Wineman (1985) write,

Many scholars have claimed the Holocaust is a unique event and in many ways an unparalleled event in human history with wide-ranging transformational consequences for the human situation.

After he Died in the World Trade Center disaster I thought back to his dreams. Our last session, on September 4, had been unexceptional. The unprecedented sporadic flashes of panic he had been feeling over the summer seemed to have subsided. There had been times when he felt suddenly claustrophobic in the subway. One time, while watching his children play with their friends in a swimming pool, he took fright that one of them had drowned, and he counted and counted over and over to assure himself, feeling silly, that all of them were there. They were. Life went on as usual, with his gladness in his children, his deepening bond with his wife, his restlessness with his job, and what had become our therapeutic puzzle: his sense that even if work were satisfactorily to engage his ambition, and if his money worries were to abate, still it might not be enough—still there would be the inevitable unreeling of time, the perpetual passing away.

And so a week passed and the terror planes flew into the towers, trapping him on a high floor on what should have been the day of our next session. He and so many others died. And I, in that ancillary position peculiar to psychoanalysis—where with him I knew his life so well yet stood outside it—I was left with the puzzling mystery of passing away. Partly out of my own sadness and loss, partly out of wanting to find him still, partly in uneasy approach to the mystery, I looked back through the cursory jottings of my notes and was jarred to remember one of his dreams.

On July 17, when sparks of anxiety could surprise him in waking life, he dreamt that he was in a dark scene, needing to flee. At first—was he in a building?—there were corridors and obstructions and then he was on rooftops, going from this one to that, and there were police, teams of police all over, not chasing him, but also going this way and that, in chaos and confusion, until somehow he found a way out and away. He found himself trying to ignite the extinguished pilot light of a hot water heater, only to realize, as it exploded, that there must have been leaking gas.

Jay Kwawer   director of clinical education, training and supervising analyst, William Alanson White Institute; clinical professor of psychology, New York University Postdoctoral Program in Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis.

Fromm's clinical approach has been transmitted largely through the oral tradition. He was always disinclined to commit to writing schematic principles for fear that they would be reified through the dogmatic religiosity of accolytes. This aspect of Fromm's corpus contrasts with the breadth of his writing as a social—rather than clinical—psychologist, which consists of almost two dozen books, some of them perennial bestsellers and fixtures on college reading lists (i.e., Fromm, 1941, 1947, 1951, 1955, 1956, 1961, 1962). Biancoli suggests that Fromm's core belief that “each individual is unique, each analytic relationship is unique, and this uniqueness is a value that might be harmed by the standardized application of rigid rules” (p. 609) is the reason he never wrote a book on psychoanalytic technique. In this sense, Fromm believed that the codification of psychoanalytic technique risked alienating clinical practice from the fundamental concern with uniqueness and individuality.

Beyond this (as a perhaps deeper and more personal motive), I suspect that Fromm' quite deliberate and intentional emancipation from his personal and professional roots in orthodox Judaism and orthodox Freudianism left him deeply suspicious of the dangers of ideas becoming systematized as the objects of idolatrous worship (Kwawer, 2000). As a consequence of this idiosyncratic inclination of Fromm's, those who speak with conviction and authority about his psychoanalytic technique do so either on the basis of first-hand encounters with Fromm as students, analysands, or supervisees (Kwawer, 1975, 1991; Landis, 1981; Tauber, 1959) or do so inferentially on the basis of a shared understanding of the basic tenets of his developmental and clinical theories.

It is a Pleasure to reply to Steve Tublin's thoughtful and considerate response to my article. Like all responses worth their salt, Tuhlin's provides much more than a simple exposition of my ideas. He brings a dialogical spirit of inquiry to bear that affirmed certain of my points, questioned others, and (best of all) challenged me to clarify and further develop the ideas raised in the article. IIis response is a welcomed opportunity for me to continue exploring, through dialogue with him and the readers of this journal, something that is otherwise completely ineffable—unconscious experience.

Questions of “depth” have always been at the heart of many a disagreement within the psychoanalytic world. Over the last century, virtually all theoretical perspectives within psychoanalysis have submitted the charge that the other theories lack insight into or appreciation of the depths of human personality and experience. Charges of lack of depth or relative superficiality often comprise the fault lines between various psychoanalytic approaches. The precise areas of emphasis (e.g., instincts, interpersonal relationships, self-cohesion, relational matrixes) vary, but constant is the preoccupation that many analysts and analytic thinkers have with wanting to know (and wanting others to know) that their approach offers the best point of access to the depths of their patients' concerns. Charging that another thinker's position does not provide a deep understanding of personality is often a way to contain or fix the other's position within the terms and parameters of one's own perspective. Nowhere is this tendency greater than discussions about “the unconscious.”

An observation that wends throughout Tublin's response to my article is that my conceptualization of the “psychoanalytic unconscious” does not account for, as he calls it, the “truly unconscious unconscious.”
